title: Setting Expectations
hook: Thirty quiet minutes before service can spare a team years of vague resentment.
counterintuition: A high bar is not pressure by itself; it becomes useful when leaders translate it into daily, observable behavior.
tryThisNow: Turn one vague standard into a sentence a new teammate could act on during the next shift.
keyTakeaway: Clear expectations make excellence repeatable because people can only rise to a standard they can see.

breakdown.fastRead: A new general manager at twenty-six walked into a kitchen split into camps. Long-tenured servers liked things loose and personal. Newer hires, drilled in fine-dining protocol, wanted everything precise. They argued about what good service even meant, and guests felt the inconsistency. The fix was not to pick a side. It was to name the standard out loud. People cannot meet a bar that has never been made visible. Excellence becomes repeatable only when the expectation is explicit, explained, repeated daily, and held with respect for the person being asked to rise.
breakdown.deepRead: Why does a vague standard breed resentment instead of effort? Because when no one names the bar, people infer it from mood and reputation, and inconsistent enforcement feels arbitrary and unfair. The cure starts with a destination. The mission set for Eleven Madison Park was to become the four-star restaurant for the next generation, as warm and unpretentious as the spots younger diners loved, yet held to the rigor of true fine dining. A concrete, memorable target makes every smaller standard legible, because people can see what they are reaching for. But a mission on a wall changes nothing by itself. The lever that made it real was a mandatory thirty-minute pre-meal meeting, held every single day. It was not used to bark orders. It aligned the team, explained the reasoning behind each task, and celebrated wins, so the standard was reinforced and re-explained on every shift. A high bar is just pressure until a leader translates it into daily, observable behavior. Said once in a meeting, a standard fades by the weekend; said and shown every day, it sticks.
breakdown.fullRead: Naming a hard standard can feel unkind, like you are about to become a tyrant. The opposite is true. Declining to name expectations, to seem easygoing, actually abandons people, because a vague bar inconsistently enforced is what breeds resentment and factions. Clarity is the kindness. People feel seen and can finally rise when they know exactly what good looks like and why it matters. Getting there took patience, not force. Before changing anything, the new manager spent months in one-on-one conversations, surfacing grievances and hidden strengths first. That listening did two things at once. It told people the new standards would be explained, not dumped on them, and it revealed talent the org charts had missed, including a struggling food runner whose leadership emerged the moment he was moved into the expediter role, where he thrived. Clarity surfaces hidden talent as often as it corrects sloppiness. Discipline was made to feel fair by being consistent and aimed at behavior, never personality. Criticism was delivered privately, praise was given systematically, and people were urged to raise problems early, before resentment could build, so they felt like vital parts of an exciting change rather than obstacles to it. Fairness, here, is not softness. It is the thing that lets a high standard hold without poisoning the room. A standard that bends depending on who is involved is the fastest way to lose the people holding it. None of this is restaurant-only. Any team drifting into inconsistency is usually guessing at a bar no one ever stated. The move is the same everywhere: name a concrete mission, translate it into explicit daily standards, reinforce it in a short repeated ritual, and enforce it the same way for everyone. A support team with wild quality swings, a sales floor where every rep invents their own rules, a classroom without a clear bar, each is usually a place where the standard was simply never stated. State it plainly, explain why it matters, and reinforce it every day, and the swings start to flatten. The limit keeps it honest. Setting expectations is not a single rousing speech or a laminated values poster. It is a daily practice of making the standard visible before judging whether people met it. The honest test is whether a normal team, on a normal day, can say what great looks like here and point to where they learned it. When it can, the standard has stopped being a mood and become something people can actually see and reach.

examples.scenario: Anneke Vos, the new general manager, takes over a divided service team at twenty-six, and the staff want to know what she is actually aiming for. She could keep things vague to seem easygoing, or name a bold, specific mission, the same one Eleven Madison Park chose when it set out to become the four-star restaurant for the next generation. A fuzzy target has already bred factions. Minutes before her first all-hands, Anneke needs to decide whether to soften the goal into something safe or name a destination clear enough for everyone to chase.
examples.whatToDo: Name a concrete, ambitious mission out loud instead of staying vague to seem easygoing, because a clear destination is what lets a divided team start chasing the same thing.
examples.whyItMatters: Without a stated target and consistent reinforcement, talented people drift into inconsistency, factions form, and correction feels arbitrary; naming the goal and explaining the reasoning turns vague effort into aligned, repeatable performance.

examples.title: Spelling it out without being a tyrant

planSpec.stakes: Taking over as general manager at twenty-six revealed a house split into factions: long-tenured staff used to relaxed, personable service clashed with newer hires drilled in precis
planSpec.requiredBeat: Apply the lesson to this situation without copying a surface gesture.

examples.scenario: 'If I spell out exactly what good looks like, won't I seem like a tyrant?' the new lead asked. Marlon Diaz, a veteran general manager, shook his head. 'Vague standards you enforce by mood are the cruelty. Clear ones are a kindness; that is how Eleven Madison Park turned a factional house into one team.' He handed her the standards sheet. 'Before tomorrow's shift, you have to decide to make one fuzzy expectation explicit and explain the why behind it.'
examples.whatToDo: Make a fuzzy expectation explicit and explain the reason behind it, because naming the standard clearly is a kindness, while leaving it vague and mood-enforced is the real cruelty.
examples.whyItMatters: Clarity is a kindness, not a cruelty: declining to name expectations in order to seem easygoing actually abandons people, because vague standards inconsistently enforced breed resentment and factions, whereas explicit standards consistently and respectfully enforced are what let people feel seen and rise.

examples.scenario: Petra Kowalski is the incoming director of a resentful, divided department, and she is tempted to impose new rules on day one to show command. The other path is slower: weeks of one-on-one listening before changing anything, the way a new leader at Eleven Madison Park surfaced grievances first so standards felt explained, not dumped on people. Her boss wants fast results. Before the reorg memo goes out Friday, Petra has to choose between imposing the fix now and listening her way to a fix the team will own.
examples.whatToDo: Listen one-on-one to surface grievances before imposing any change, because standards that are explained and co-owned hold, while standards dumped on people only breed resentment.
examples.whyItMatters: A more complex, time-intensive menu against the same large seating count stretched timing, lengthened waits, and frustrated guests, so the inconsistency was treated as a structural problem instead of an excuse for blame.

examples.title: The huddle that flattened the swings

planSpec.stakes: Months of one-on-one listening came before any change, surfacing grievances and helping people understand that expectations would be clearly laid out and explained instead of simpl
planSpec.requiredBeat: Apply the lesson to this situation without copying a surface gesture.

examples.scenario: Before, the call-center team lead Hugh Ferris ran things on scattered emails and surprise rule changes, and quality swung wildly by shift. After Hugh borrowed the daily pre-meal ritual that Eleven Madison Park used, a short standing huddle each day to align the team, explain the why, and celebrate one win, the standards finally stuck. The huddle, not a new policy, became the lever. Within a quarter the team could say what great looked like, and the wild swings flattened out.
examples.whatToDo: Install a short daily ritual to align the team, explain the why, and celebrate a win, because a repeated gathering, not a one-time policy, is what makes standards actually stick.
examples.whyItMatters: A specific, ambitious, memorable mission gives a team a shared target that makes every downstream standard and decision legible.

examples.scenario: Morale had cratered, so the department manager Sade Okonkwo reviewed the quarter Monday with her HR partner. She had corrected people in front of the team, praised unevenly, and let standards bend by who was involved. Reading the complaints, Sade saw the pattern: her discipline felt personal and arbitrary, not fair. Like the approach that united Eleven Madison Park, criticism should have been private and aimed at behavior, praise systematic, and problems raised early, so people felt like contributors instead of targets.
examples.whatToDo: Aim criticism at behavior in private and give praise systematically, applying the same standard to everyone, because discipline that feels personal or arbitrary destroys the trust it needs.
examples.whyItMatters: A high bar is not pressure by itself; it becomes useful when leaders translate it into daily, observable behavior.

examples.scenario: Two weeks before he finalizes the new org chart, Tariq Bishara, a department director, must decide where one struggling employee goes. The obvious move is to manage her out. The other is to look harder for latent strength and place her where it can meet the standard, the way patient listening at Eleven Madison Park turned a struggling food runner into a thriving expediter. The numbers say cut. Tariq weighs writing her off against finding the role that actually fits her.
examples.whatToDo: Before writing off a struggling person, look for latent strength and place them where it can meet the standard, because patient listening often reveals potential a quick cut would waste.
examples.whyItMatters: Clear expectations make excellence repeatable because people can only rise to a standard they can see.

questions.prompt: A new team lead inherits a group with no clear target, just 'do good work.' Performance is inconsistent and people pull in different directions. What does setting expectations call for first?
choices: Name one concrete, ambitious mission everyone can aim at, since a team can only chase greatness once the destination is clear.
Keep the goal loose so no one feels pressured, since vague targets tend to keep morale comfortable.
Add more rules about daily tasks, because detailed rules matter more than any overall direction.
questions.explanation: A team can only chase greatness once the destination is named. A concrete mission gives every downstream standard meaning, while a vague target lets factions and drift take hold.

questions.prompt: A manager avoids spelling out standards because she thinks being explicit will make her seem harsh, yet her team is resentful and inconsistent. What best explains the resentment?
choices: The team resents having any standards at all, so the manager should drop expectations and let people self-direct.
The resentment is unrelated to her vagueness and probably comes from pay, not from unclear standards.
Vague standards enforced by mood breed resentment; clear, explained expectations would actually feel like fairness.
questions.explanation: Declining to name expectations does not feel easygoing; it abandons people. Standards that are vague and inconsistently enforced breed resentment, while explicit ones consistently applied feel fair.

questions.prompt: You take over a divided department and want to introduce new standards. Eager to show command, you consider issuing rules on day one. What approach better fits setting expectations?
choices: Issue the rules immediately, since a fast, firm start is the surest way to earn a divided team's respect.
Avoid standards altogether for a few months, because any change will only deepen the existing divisions.
Spend time listening one-on-one first, so the standards you set are explained and owned instead of imposed.
questions.explanation: Patient one-on-one listening surfaces grievances and helps people understand standards will be explained, not dumped on them. That groundwork is what makes new expectations hold in a divided house.

questions.prompt: A remote support team gets standards by sporadic email blasts, and quality swings wildly between shifts. You want one durable mechanism. Which fits the daily-ritual idea?
choices: Hold a short daily huddle to align the team, explain the why, and celebrate a win, so the standard is reinforced every day.
Send a longer, more detailed email once a month, since thorough written rules are what create consistency.
Post the standards on a wall and assume people will absorb them on their own over time.
questions.explanation: A repeated daily gathering, not a one-time message, is the central lever of culture. It aligns the team, explains the reasoning, and celebrates wins, which is what makes standards stick.

questions.prompt: When a leader praises unevenly, corrects people publicly, and bends rules depending on who is involved, morale sinks. A peer says the discipline itself is the problem. How should you evaluate that?
choices: Disagree, since strong discipline naturally lowers morale and the dip is just the price of high standards.
Agree: discipline that feels personal and arbitrary destroys trust, while private, behavior-focused correction feels fair.
Disagree, because morale depends only on pay and workload, not on how discipline is delivered.
questions.explanation: Discipline is made fair by being consistent and aimed at behavior, not personality. Public, uneven correction reads as arbitrary; private criticism plus systematic praise keeps it feeling just.

questions.prompt: A food runner keeps underperforming in his role, and the obvious move is to let him go. A patient manager instead discovers a strength and moves him. What does this illustrate about expectations?
choices: That underperformers should be given endless chances, since no one should be moved out of a role for poor results.
That patient listening can surface latent strength, and placing a person where it meets the standard beats writing them off.
That roles are fixed, so a struggling person should be coached harder in the same role until they improve.
questions.explanation: Patient one-on-one attention can reveal potential a quick cut would waste. Seeing a struggling runner's latent leadership and moving him to expediter let him meet the standard where he fit.

questions.prompt: A coworker contends, 'Real leaders stay flexible and avoid pinning down hard expectations, because rigid standards just stress people out.' How should you assess that?
choices: Agree fully, since the most beloved leaders are the ones who hold no one to a written standard.
Agree, because firm expectations tend to create stress, and a stress-free team is the higher goal.
Push back: refusing to name expectations abandons people, while clear standards consistently held are a kindness, not a stressor.
questions.explanation: Clarity is a kindness, not cruelty. Vague standards inconsistently enforced are what breed stress and resentment; explicit, fairly enforced expectations give people a target and a sense of fairness.

questions.prompt: You are launching a new team and want expectations that motivate instead of just instructing. What is the strongest design?
choices: Hand out a thick rulebook on day one, since the most detailed instructions produce the most motivated team.
Build a short daily ritual where you connect each standard to the mission and explain the why behind the task.
Set the rules silently and let people discover the reasons themselves through trial and error over months.
questions.explanation: Expectations stick when people understand the reasoning and see them tied to a mission. A daily ritual that explains the why and celebrates progress motivates far more than a silent rulebook.

questions.prompt: You run a city library branch drifting without direction. You want to set expectations the way a strong leader would. What is the best first move?
choices: Name a vivid, ambitious mission for the branch, then translate it into a few clear daily standards the team can chase.
Copy another famous library's mission word for word, since a borrowed mission saves time and still works.
Skip the mission and just tighten attendance rules, because punctuality is what really drives a library's value.
questions.explanation: A team can only aim once the destination is named. Setting a concrete mission and translating it into daily standards gives a drifting branch the shared target it has been missing.

reviewCards.front: Beyond hoping a team performs, what must a leader name and translate into clear daily standards?
reviewCards.back: Name a concrete, ambitious mission, then translate it into explicit daily standards and a short repeated ritual, because people can only rise to a standard they can actually see.

reviewCards.front: What does a team splitting into factions reveal about where its standards fall short?
reviewCards.back: It reveals that the standard was never made explicit, so vague expectations inconsistently enforced bred resentment and camps; clarity, not easygoing vagueness, is the missing kindness.

reviewCards.front: Why does a short daily alignment ritual transfer from a restaurant to a call center or a clinic?
reviewCards.back: Because expectations stick only through a repeated, structured ritual that communicates both the standard and the why, so any team that needs consistency benefits from that daily reinforcement.

reviewCards.front: What is the most common way leaders leave the bar to mood, reputation, or tradition?
reviewCards.back: They never state the standard explicitly, so the team has to guess it from the leader's mood and reputation, and inconsistent enforcement makes every correction feel arbitrary and unfair.

reviewCards.front: What single question helps a manager coach clear expectations without sounding like a tyrant?
reviewCards.back: Ask: 'Have we actually named what great looks like here and explained why, or are people guessing the bar from our mood?'

reviewCards.front: A mission statement can gather dust. What makes a team actually live up to a named standard?
reviewCards.back: When the mission is translated into explicit standards, reinforced in a daily ritual that explains the why, and discipline is fair, private, and aimed at behavior.

implementationPlan.title: Setting Expectations Practice
implementationPlan.coreSkill: Name a concrete, ambitious mission, then translate it into explicit daily standards and a short repeated ritual where you explain the why and celebrate wins. Listen one-on-one before imposing change, and aim discipline at behavior in private while praising systematically, because clear, fairly enforced expectations are a kindness, not a cruelty.

ifThenPlans.context: Performance swings shift to shift because no one has actually named what good looks like.
ifThenPlans.plan: If the service works on paper, then name the feeling it should create and adjust one step before repeating it.

ifThenPlans.context: A bold mission statement becomes a poster nobody translates into daily behavior.
ifThenPlans.plan: If the team copies the surface detail, then pause and identify the human need the story addressed.

ifThenPlans.context: Pressure revives the old habit: expect people to infer the bar from mood, reputation, or tradition.
ifThenPlans.plan: If the old habit returns, then protect one small behavior that keeps the receiver's experience visible.

ifThenPlans.context: Spotting one person's hidden strength makes the whole team want to aim higher.
ifThenPlans.plan: If the idea feels exciting, then ask whether it will make the person feel confident about what excellence looks like or merely make the team feel clever.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Pick one fuzzy expectation your team is guessing at and make it explicit today, explaining the why behind it, then watch whether performance tightens up.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Review three exchanges through setting expectations: one that worked, one that missed, and one that could improve with a smaller, sharper change.
